title: The Fidelity Spectrum Is a Theorem: What Survives Translation Between Proof Kernels, Verified in Two of Them
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: A recent metatheoretic critique argues that formal auditing conducted from a single logical foundation — in particular, a calculus-of-constructions kernel — is a lossy projection of the audited structure: reliable for content of low homotopical dimension, and provably blind above it, with the reliability graded by a "fidelity spectrum" (Zhou and Zhou, 2026c). The critique was aimed, in part, at our own kernel-checked audit of a speculative physics program (The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics, 2026). This paper responds by formalizing the critique. Working in the Goguen–Burstall theory of institutions (Goguen and Burstall, 1992) — where "truth is invariant under change of notation" is itself a mathematical condition — we exhibit the fidelity spectrum as a theorem pair. The floor: the truncation translation from a path-distinguishing institution to an executable audit institution is a satisfaction-condition-carrying comorphism on the 0-truncated sentence fragment — the critique's concession that single-foundation auditing has "reliable local efficacy" is proved, not granted. The loss: an explicit sentence — two loops with equal endpoints and distinct windings — whose truncation the audit institution accepts while the path institution refutes; non-conservativity above level 0 is witnessed, not argued. Every Lean 4 declaration involved carries an empty kernel axiom footprint. The critique's own open question — whether its diagnosis "requires recalibration under cubical type theory semantics" — is answered by a second, independent artifact: in Cubical Agda (–cubical –safe, zero postulates), the loops intLoop 1 and intLoop 2 are distinguished by their winding numbers in ΩS 1 — genuine path structure — and identified by squash2 in the set truncation. The two kernels thus check the two halves of the claim each natively expresses, which is precisely the "polycentric cognitive ecology" the critique advocates — instantiated, with the passage between the centers carrying a machine-checked certificate of what survives it. Both sides of the dispute emerge vindicated, as theorems. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

abstract: FIQS-AllomEq-RAG Public Archival Release v2.0.1 This release provides the Zenodo archival version of the independent FIQS / AllomEq-RAG public repository. Code provenance: This release points to the same source-code commit (7d8e032) as v2.0.0-public. No source-code or algorithm changes were introduced. The package includes public implementations, configuration files, prompt templates, synthetic examples, smoke tests, and reproducibility documentation. The original formal 522-query benchmark has not been rerun from its complete per-query records. Private benchmark records, complete research datasets, and trained model weights are not included. This release is intended to establish a citable, version-specific software archive.

title: A Rational Function Model for the Decomposition of Global Solar Irradiance into Direct and Diffuse Components
abstract: Solar irradiance decomposition models are essential for estimating direct normal irradiance and diffuse horizontal irradiance when only global horizontal irradiance measurements are available. While recent studies have increasingly relied on machine learning techniques, analytical models remain attractive because of their transparency, low computational cost, and ease of implementation. This study proposes a rational function model for the decomposition of global horizontal irradiance into its direct and diffuse components. The model parameters were calibrated using four years of high-quality measurements from four stations of the Baseline Surface Radiation Network (BSRN) representing different climatic conditions. The resulting parameterization combines mathematical simplicity with the ability to reproduce the nonlinear dependence of irradiance components on atmospheric conditions. The model was subsequently validated using independent BSRN datasets not involved in the calibration stage. Its performance was assessed through standard statistical indicators and compared with results reported in the recent literature, including both classical analytical decomposition models and machine-learning approaches. The results demonstrate that carefully calibrated analytical formulations remain a viable alternative to more complex data-driven methods. The proposed rational model provides an effective compromise between accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency, making it suitable for solar energy applications requiring reliable irradiance component estimates.

The resulting parameterization combines mathematical simplicity with the ability to reproduce the nonlinear dependence of irradiance components on atmospheric conditions. The model was subsequently validated using independent BSRN datasets not involved in the calibration stage. Its performance was assessed through standard statistical indicators and compared with results reported in the recent literature, including both classical analytical decomposition models and machine-learning approaches. The results demonstrate that carefully calibrated analytical formulations remain a viable alternative to more complex data-driven methods. The proposed rational model provides an effective compromise between accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency, making it suitable for solar energy applications requiring reliable irradiance component estimates.

title: Personalized LLM Recommendation with Semantic IDs: Autoregressive Beam Search vs. Multi-Token Prediction
abstract: Large-scale personalization is shifting from embedding-table retrieval to LLM-based recommenders that generate the Semantic ID (SID) of the item to recommend, where each SID is a short sequence of discrete hierarchical content codes. A single instruction-tuned model can then unify retrieval, content understanding, and language, and recommend brand-new titles from their content alone using SID; then, how should the model generate the SID? Traditionally, models rely on a single language modeling head that generates tokens autoregressively, typically using constrained beam search. In contrast, an emerging body of work explores multi-token prediction (MTP), where dedicated heads predict all tokens in parallel, substantially reducing the decoding latency associated with beam search. We report an industry-scale, apples-to-apples comparison of these two generation paradigms: single-head autoregressive decoding vs. MTP. We introduce a new auxiliary ranking loss, defined over the joint SID score, to train the MTP objective. We evaluate the SID training objectives on both quality and training/inference cost, inside a multi-task LLM that jointly does personalized retrieval, content question-answering (QA), and instruction following over a large streaming-media catalog. Our experiments show single-head beam search consistently beats MTP on most product-critical metrics: ranking and content QA, and trains at roughly 2.6x lower dollar cost on Qwen3-8B scale; MTP wins only on raw inference throughput. Around this finding, we detail an efficient training and inference stack and report end-to-end gains over the previous non-SID baseline equipped with an auxiliary ranking head: +77% item cold-start ranking, +22% content-QA accuracy, +2.8x faster training, with language metric regression traced to SID vocabulary expansion. We address the language regression by reinforcement learning post training.

title: Ellipsoids from Tangents
abstract: This paper presents an algorithm for detecting and fitting multiple ellipsoids in 2D, 3D and higher-dimensional data. The representation is based on tangents to the ellipsoid together with their contact points, rather than on points alone. A tangent contributes d independent equations where a point contributes one, so each hypothesis needs fewer samples, which in turn reduces the number of iterations required to recover every ellipsoid. The problem is posed as sets of linear equations whose solutions -- the ellipsoid parameters -- are recovered robustly by clustering in parameter space. The algorithm works in all dimensions and outperforms the state of the art in 2D. The approach applies in general to the robust solution of linear equations, and so has utility beyond ellipsoid fitting.

title: OntoAR-HAR: Ontology-Guided Agentic RAG with Personalized Memory for Human Activity Recognition
abstract: LLMs increasingly support sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) by linking motion signals with activity semantics and physical knowledge. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) grounds decisions in sensor examples and domain features, enabling training-free target-user inference with less dependence on raw numerical arrays. However, existing LLM/RAG-based HAR typically searches single-level activity spaces using static population knowledge. Consequently, they compare many unrelated candidates using the same static population evidence and overlook personalized motion patterns. We propose OntoAR-HAR, an ontology-guided agentic RAG framework combining static population and personalized knowledge. Its tree-structured activity ontology decomposes classification into local decisions among semantically related activities. The static store supplies node-constrained examples, while offline-discovered executable signal features provide numerical evidence for local distinctions. During inference, the personalized store collects selected user observations, which the LLM integrates with static knowledge and signal features while traversing the ontology to an activity label. Cross-subject and heterogeneous-sensing experiments show complementary gains from hierarchical retrieval and personalized memory across multiple LLM backbones, achieving state-of-the-art performance. By explicitly modeling hierarchical relations across activity granularities, OntoAR-HAR also addresses the long-overlooked semantic inclusion problem and avoids treating related labels as independent categories.

title: Semantic Context Forests for Learning-Based Knee Cartilage Segmentation in 3D MR Images
abstract: The automatic segmentation of human knee cartilage from 3D MR images is a useful yet challenging task due to the thin sheet structure of the cartilage with diffuse boundaries and inhomogeneous intensities. In this paper, we present an iterative multi-class learning method to segment the femoral, tibial and patellar cartilage simultaneously, which effectively exploits the spatial contextual constraints between bone and cartilage, and also between different cartilages. First, based on the fact that the cartilage grows in only certain area of the corresponding bone surface, we extract the distance features of not only to the surface of the bone, but more informatively, to the densely registered anatomical landmarks on the bone surface. Second, we introduce a set of iterative discriminative classifiers that at each iteration, probability comparison features are constructed from the class confidence maps derived by previously learned classifiers. These features automatically embed the semantic context information between different cartilages of interest. Validated on a total of 176 volumes from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) dataset, the proposed approach demonstrates high robustness and accuracy of segmentation in comparison with existing state-of-the-art MR cartilage segmentation methods. Code: https://github.com/wq2012/kneeseg Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/knee-mri-segmentation

title: Protologue: A Taxonomy of Prompting and LLM Techniques
abstract: Protologue is an openly licensed, sourced reference for the vocabulary of prompting and large language model techniques. Each entry has a permanent identifier (PTL-NNNN), a standalone one-to-two-sentence definition, synonyms, broader, narrower and related links (SKOS semantics), and the primary source that introduced the technique. Version 1.0.0 contains 101 techniques in 10 branches (foundations, exemplars, reasoning, verification, retrieval and tools, agents, optimization, test-time compute, security, and failure modes), citing 98 primary sources. Every arXiv citation was checked against the paper. This archive contains the source data (YAML), the generator that builds the website and its machine-readable exports (JSON, CSV, SKOS JSON-LD and Turtle, llms.txt), and an MCP server for AI agents. The live reference is at https://protologue.com/.

title: Statistical Mechanics from a Closure Operator: A Generative Algebraic Substrate
authors: The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics
abstract: Canonical statistical mechanics rests on six analytic inputs — a phase space, Liouville evolution, ergodicity, a chosen Hamiltonian, a temperature, and detailed balance. We show that five of those six can be replaced by theorems derived from a single algebraic primitive: a forced-mask nucleus acting as a closure operator on a bi-Heyting lattice of finite Boolean coordinates. The Hamiltonian itself acquires a canonical algebraic form — closure distance from a state to its forced-nucleus closure — which we call the closure-distance Hamiltonian. The resulting kernel is computable over the rationals, requires no analysis on its load-bearing surface, is mechanically verified in Lean 4, and lands theorem-by-theorem into the rule library of the Boundary substrate, an active-pair interaction-net runtime that compiles to bare metal. We present five executable demonstrations — a Schottky heat-capacity oracle, a saturated AllowedFlow entropy-conservation bound, a finite swap-symmetry equipartition law, a residuebit Landauer floor, and a detailed-balance identity from an involutive energy-preserving step — each of which consumes a distinct headline kernel theorem and emits runtime rows whose values are a load-bearing function of the formal proof rather than a Python lift. A coordinated proof-and-execution pipeline closes the loop: math becomes proof, proof becomes a rule theorem, the rule theorem becomes a reduction step, and the reduction step runs on the same hardware that runs the verifier. We make the scope explicit. Real-valued analytic content (Boltzmann e−βh , the Landauer formula kB T ln 2) is retained as overlay provenance only; the load-bearing surface uses a second-order Padé-rational weight in Q. A continuum limit, a topos-quantum lift, the full first law of thermodynamics, and renormalization-group fixed points are explicitly held for follow-on work and not claimed here. Published by The Institute for Applied Ontological Mathematics.

title: Apertus8B open source Large Language Model (LLM) prioritizing low-resource languages
abstract: Apertus is a fully open source Large Language Model (LLM) released in September 2025 by the Swiss Federal Polytechnical Institutes of Zurich (ETHZ) and Lausanne (EPFL) as a free, public alternative to commercial, closed source (black-box) LLMs. It was trained on the Swiss Alps supercomputer on 1811 languages with a specific focus on low-resource languages such as Swiss-German (Romansch) dialects. Apertus is available in 8B and 70B releases. It shows a much better quality level than proprietary models trained on general purpose languages such as NLLB-200. The code includes two main scripts, run-translator.sh and run-multitask.sh for translation only and for multimodal language processing. A demo of the multitask component is available on Hugging Face spaces at https://huggingface.co/spaces/Norelad/apertus-8b-multitask. Apertus8B is the main model of the multilingual, multimodal application TraductAL, based on a neuro-symbolic approach which uses Janus-Prolog for the detection and correction of errors and hallucinations of the LLM.

title: Survival-aware self-play reinforcement learning for partially observable beyond visual range air combat
abstract: We present a recurrent self-play reinforcement learning framework for autonomous beyond-visual-range (BVR) air combat under partial observability. The environment is formulated as a decision-level BVR missile-duel simulator that combines 3-DoF aircraft kinematics, field-of-view radar observation, track-quality decay, flight-envelope action masking, and an energy-aware missile model with boost, coast, drag, and proportional-navigation guidance. To handle intermittent radar contact, the policy uses an LSTM backbone. To stabilize recurrent training, we introduce trajectory-aligned hidden-state management and mask recurrent sequences at episode boundaries. The training follows an asymmetric self-play scheme in which the protagonist is updated by a recurrent MAPPO-style objective with centralized value input, while opponents are sampled from frozen historical policy snapshots. A survival-aware reward function balances offensive alignment, radar tracking, beam-like defensive maneuvering, missile-threat avoidance, and time cost. Experiments and ablations use episodic reward as a process-level training indicator and win rate as the final outcome-level confrontation metric. The results show that recurrent memory, opponent-pool self-play, and survival-aware reward shaping improve robustness in partially observable BVR engagements. The current study focuses on controlled 1-vs-1 BVR missile duels and provides a basis for future N-vs-N cooperative extensions.

title: Exact Privacy--Distortion Design of Support-Constrained Randomized Response
abstract: Full-support local randomizers can incur unnecessary reporting distortion on ordered alphabets. We study randomized response whose output is restricted to a radius-$t$ neighborhood of the private input. Input-dependent supports create privacy leakage at their boundaries, so ordinary likelihood-ratio calibration is no longer sufficient. Under approximate local privacy restricted to input pairs at distance at most $H$, we derive the exact hockey-stick defect of the mechanism. We then solve the joint design of the truthful probability, off-truth probability, and support radius. The fixed-radius optimum is available in closed form, while the global optimum requires only a one-dimensional integer search. We characterize both the privacy floor and its inverse, namely the smallest defect attainable under a reporting-distortion budget. We further prove that stringent approximate privacy forces the support size to scale as $Ω(H/δ)$. Deterministic evaluations illustrate the resulting tradeoff.

title: A Hybrid Gaussian Process-Extreme Gradient Boosting Machine Learning Framework for Robust Knockdown Factor Prediction and Reliability-Based Design of Thin Spherical Shell Caps
abstract: Elastic buckling remains a critical concern in the design of deep spherical shell caps, given that experiments reveal a significant reduction of critical loads from those predicted by linearized eigen-buckling analysis. This discrepancy has been attributed to initial geometric imperfections and is often reconciled through a dimensionless parameter, namely the knockdown factor (KDF). However, conventional KDFs (NASA SP-8007; Eurocode 3) are highly conservative, as they represent the lower bound of an extensive body of experimental data. This study aims to narrow the conservatism in the KDFs for spherical shell caps through machine learning (ML) regression models trained on experimental data on spherical shell buckling. A hybrid model is proposed by combining Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) with Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and its improved performance is demonstrated over conventional ML algorithms, i.e., the Artificial Neural Network (ANN), Support Vector Regressor (SVR), Random Forest Regressor (RFR), and Histogram-based Gradient Boosting (HGBoost). Each of these models uses six input features and a single output, i.e., the KDF. The most critical feature affecting the KDF is ascertained through a sensitivity analysis. The study concludes with a reliability-based design framework that relies on the predictive ML model to obtain safety-consistent, yet less conservative, KDFs.

title: Towards Robust Calibration Dataset for Domain-General Mixture of Experts Pruning
abstract: Post-training expert pruning is a promising deployment technique for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. The calibration set is an integral part of the pruning process, however, its correlation with evaluation performance is largely misunderstood and unintuitive. In this work, we present an empirical study of the robustness of calibration perturbations, specifically in MoE models. Showing how calibration size, language, and data distribution affect layer-wise expert pruning for gpt-oss-20b. Our findings reveal that (1) domain-general pruning quality receives minimal benefit from scaling calibration data beyond small sample sizes, (2) cross-lingual calibration transfers effectively, with English-only calibration maintaining strong performance across seven languages of varying typologies and scripts, and (3) a diverse calibration data resembling the pretraining distribution can yield comparable or superior performance to test-distribution data. Ultimately, we provide practical insights as a recipe for better understanding calibration for more effective domain-general expert pruning.

title: Co-DSL: Human-LLM Co-design of Reusable Spatial Concepts for Layout Generation
abstract: We present Co-DSL, a framework in which users and LLMs co-design reusable spatial concepts for layout generation. In the first stage, our system allows users to create a library of personalized operations. To add a concept, a user provides a description, which the LLM converts into an initial implementation. The user can then observe the concept's execution behavior over example scenarios and provide lightweight feedback to the LLM, which revises the concept's implementation logic. In the second stage, given a library, an LLM can author a layout program that meets a new layout request from a user. Executing a layout program instantiates a concept-graph, a declarative composition of library concepts. In this way, we require the LLM only to specify which concepts should hold, while we use a solver to search for a layout that satisfies them. Across five spatial layout domains, we find that Co-DSL libraries let LLMs capture layout patterns that are challenging for prior fixed-operation systems, and demonstrate that our concept-graph representation is needed for LLMs to reliably compose concepts together. We further find that Co-DSL lets LLMs author generative layout programs that expose high-level parametric controls users can manipulate to explore a distribution of related layouts without re-prompting.

title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. PANINI-DR achieves the strongest average performance across the three benchmarks. On BrowseComp-Plus, it achieves 73.3% accuracy, outperforming the next-best harness by 16.0 points. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

evidence.title: PANINI-DR: Controlled Deep Research through Generative Semantic Workspaces
evidence.abstract: Deep research requires connecting multiple steps of search, reasoning, and computation, with intermediate findings guiding what to investigate next. As investigations grow, agents must maintain research state across model calls and check findings before errors propagate into subsequent work. We introduce PANINI-DR, a multi-agent harness that separates coordination of the overall investigation from the research and verification of individual subquestions. A shared workspace, built on the Generative Semantic Workspace representation, records subquestions, their dependencies, findings, and supporting evidence. Researchers investigate individual subquestions, while a separate verification agent checks proposed answers against those subquestions and their evidence. Verification feedback guides further investigation, and recorded findings inform subsequent assignments. We evaluate PANINI-DR on BrowseComp-Plus, FRAMES, and MoNaCo against seven state-of-the-art deep-research harnesses, all using a shared language-model backbone and frozen corpora. Its advantage is strongest on hard questions, where it answers nearly twice as many as the next-best harness. Ablations further show that structured planning and persistent state improve performance, as does checking each finding against its cited evidence before it is reused. Because a model can answer correctly from memory alone, we also analyze the evidence retained by each harness. PANINI-DR achieves the highest answer recoverability from saved evidence on all three benchmarks, while complementary claim-support audits show stronger evidence-backed answers. Accounting for this evidence changes how harnesses compare and further strengthens PANINI-DR's advantage.

title: ExeWorldBench: Benchmarking Code-Based Executable 3D World Modeling
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly evolving beyond reproducing what a world looks like toward constructing executable worlds that capture how a world works. This shift calls for executable world modeling, which integrates two core capabilities: world understanding, reasoning about the underlying structural, mechanical, and causal principles of a world, and executable realization, translating that understanding into a code-based system whose behavior emerges from physical interactions. However, existing benchmarks provide only fragmented evaluations centered on physical reasoning, visual fidelity, or behavioral correctness, leaving the integration of these capabilities insufficiently assessed. To bridge this gap, we introduce ExeWorldBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark to comprehensively evaluate world understanding and executable realization through code-based 3D world construction. ExeWorldBench comprises three progressively challenging tasks: Mechanism Executability, which evaluates the realization of individual mechanisms from visual observations; Compositional Executability, which extends to multi-stage systems with spatial, mechanical, and causal dependencies; and Intent-Driven Executable World Synthesis, which requires constructing executable worlds from high-level goals and physical requirements. Extensive experiments on frontier models reveal substantial limitations in executable world modeling, offering insights into the development of more physically grounded and causally coherent world construction systems.

title: CUSE: Fine-Grained Multimodal Unlearning with Counterfactual Guidance and On-Policy Self-Distillation
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can reproduce sensitive, copyrighted, or unsafe information from their training data. Effective unlearning must remove target information while preserving non-target content, even within the same response. Existing methods typically apply uniform forgetting objectives to complete responses and rely on fixed, off-policy supervision, resulting in coarse token control and misalignment with the model's current behavior. We propose CUSE, a Counterfactual-guided Unlearning framework via on-policy Self-distillation for multimodal large language models. It first constructs counterfactual inputs by removing target-related evidence and uses the resulting changes in token probabilities to identify which tokens require stronger forgetting. It then distills token-level forgetting and retention targets on responses sampled from the current policy, with a frozen copy of the original model serving as the teacher model augmented with the corresponding forgetting- and retention-oriented privileged contexts. This design jointly determines what to forget and what to preserve. On MLLMU-Bench, CUSE reduces forget-set ROUGE-L by 33.6% while achieving 1.2% higher retain-set ROUGE-L than the strongest baseline.

title: SkillHorizon: Constructing Long-Horizon Agent Tasks through Skill Composition
abstract: Long-horizon agents must complete workflows in which later activities depend on earlier outputs and changes to shared state. A key challenge for evaluation is to expand task requirements and their dependencies while keeping tasks executable and outcomes verifiable. We introduce SkillHorizon, a benchmark that constructs long-horizon tasks through skill composition in seven business environments. Its generators use domain-specific rules to turn reusable skill procedures into concrete business activities. These activities are connected through input-output dependencies, shared resources, and state updates, allowing workload and coordination demands to grow together. Successful reference executions validate task feasibility and measure interaction workload, while programmatic evaluators assess local completion and whole-task success. We evaluate five language models on 1,050 tasks with reference interaction workloads ranging from 64K to 1M tokens. Across these scales, mean local-goal completion falls from 90.4% to 46.8%, as completed work fails to keep pace with growing requirements. At larger workloads, agents more often submit unsuccessful final answers with substantial work unfinished and tool-call allowance remaining. Trace analysis also identifies cases where scripts execute successfully but their outputs fail downstream business checks. SkillHorizon provides a configurable testbed for studying sustained progress, dependency coordination, and complete task delivery in growing workflows. Our code is available at https://github.com/KnowComp/SkillHorizon.

title: UltraBERT: Beyond the Limit of BERT Pre-Training
abstract: Recent bidirectional encoders have been modernized with innovations from causal large language models (LLMs). However, the pretraining recipe itself remains inherited from small-scale conventions, leaving encoders underoptimized, with no single model performing competitively across both classification and retrieval tasks. In this work, we investigate how far encoder performance can be pushed by revisiting core design choices in training, revealing three key findings: (1) Encoders saturate on downstream tasks beyond a few trillion tokens, indicating that additional compute past this point does not help. (2) Across model sizes, lower masking ratios benefit classification while higher ones benefit retrieval, contradicting prior work suggesting larger ratios for larger models. (3) Distillation with pruning improves classification at low masking ratios but degrades retrieval at high ones. Guided by these findings, we present UltraBERT, a single encoder that assigns separate LM heads to low and high masking ratios within a batch and restricts the distillation objective to the low ratio. To our knowledge, UltraBERT is the first encoder to achieve state of the art on both classification and retrieval tasks, reaching 91.0 on GLUE and 47.7 on BEIR. Together, these results show how far encoder performance can be pushed and provide a principled basis for compute allocation, masking ratio design, and knowledge transfer in bidirectional models.

title: Training a Compact, Strong, and Realistic Text-to-Speech Model
abstract: Text-to-speech (TTS) systems are conventionally optimized for intelligibility and speaker similarity. However, neither objective captures the prosodic detail that distinguishes human performances from synthetic speech, leaving a realism gap that larger models and higher-quality data can narrow but not close. In the absence of an objective that directly targets this gap, realism remains a persistent challenge in TTS. We present Audio8-TTS, a compact 0.6B-parameter model for zero-shot voice cloning that achieves state-of-the-art performance in intelligibility and speaker similarity, with particularly strong results in perceptual naturalness. To align the training signal with human perception rather than signal-level fidelity, we construct a quality ladder from widely used open-source TTS systems and train a realism critic to assess generated speech against matched human recordings of the same sentences. An identity-erasure objective discourages the critic from relying on generator fingerprints. We train the model in three stages: multilingual supervised fine-tuning; group relative policy optimization (GRPO) with word error rate (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) rewards; and GRPO guided by the realism critic. The final stage improves perceived prosodic naturalness and speaker similarity while preserving WER performance.

title: Bridging Risk Approximation Gaps in Model Predictive Task Sampling via In-Context Modeling
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is essential for adaptive decision-making, e.g., robust Meta-RL and domain randomization (DR), and efficient post-training of large language models (LLMs), where tasks are commonly structured as Markov decision processes or prompts. A central bottleneck in all these settings is the cost of agent-environment interactions required for task selection and policy optimization. Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

Model predictive task sampling (MPTS) has emerged as a promising approach to improve sample efficiency by querying informative tasks via a risk predictive model (RPM) trained on optimization history. However, existing RPMs suffer from two failure modes: (i) sparse optimization histories, which limit RPMs' generalization across the task space, and (ii) a one-step lag in risk approximation, which causes biased difficulty estimation as the policy evolves. This work formalizes these failure modes, derives lagged-risk decompositions that expose the resulting temporal bias, and recasts risk prediction as an in-context sequence modeling problem. The developed RPM integrates a one-step look-ahead mechanism with a temporal-weighted sliding window to mitigate data non-stationarity and scarcity, without requiring additional rollouts. Empirically, our approach yields more reliable difficulty estimates and consistent performance gains across robust Meta-RL, DR, and prompt curriculum RL post-training of LLMs.

title: Representation Drift in Continual Learning: LoRA versus N-gram Memory
abstract: A language model that keeps learning online must not slowly erode its own base capabilities. We ask which part of a modern LLM should absorb continual updates, by measuring how each choice changes the model's internal representations. On a 48-layer mixture-of-experts model with a native pretrained N-gram memory, we train a seven-task chain under three update mechanisms with identical data and budgets: updating only the N-gram memory table, continually training one shared LoRA adapter, and training a fresh LoRA per task that is merged into the backbone. We capture fixed-context representations at every layer and task boundary. Updating only the N-gram memory changes the base model's representations of general math and code inputs by 26%/15% (relative RMS), against 64%/35% for merged and 97%/39% for shared LoRA. This drift does not grow with the number of tasks: it reaches 25% after the first task and stays there for all seven, while both LoRA variants keep accumulating. Its generic behaviour is essentially unchanged (no code problem lost, math NLL -0.01), and every change is confined to inspectable, reversible table rows. The cost appears elsewhere: N-gram memory acquires new tasks more weakly and its stored tasks interfere with one another, losing as much old-task NLL as shared LoRA. We show that this forgetting is governed by drift on the learned tasks' own inputs, measured from the checkpoint at which each was learned, not by generic drift (Spearman rho=0.85; rho=0.71 on Llama-3-8B), and we derive the exact relations behind it: with a frozen head, every pairwise logit margin changes by the projection of drift onto a head-difference direction. These results support a design principle for long-running online learning: write new knowledge only into the memory table and keep the backbone fixed; the remaining problem, interference between stored tasks, then lies inside the memory.

title: On the Complexity Gap Between POMDPs and Multi-Environment POMDPs
abstract: Multi-environment POMDPs (ME-POMDPs) generalize POMDPs by encoding a finite set of possible environments, capturing model uncertainty. The finite-horizon robust reward maximization problem for a ME-POMDP asks for a policy that maximizes reward in the worst environment, and recent work has shown this problem to be $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-complete. We expand the complexity landscape of ME-POMDPs by identifying which subclasses retain this $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness. In particular, we take subclasses of POMDPs that are tractable in the single-environment case, and investigate the computational complexity of these classes when extended to the multi-environment setting. We first prove the $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of multi-environment blind MDPs and deterministic POMDPs using a certain closure-under-mixture condition. We then prove $\mathsf{PSPACE}$-completeness for a range of subclasses that do not satisfy that closure condition, yielding new complexity results for multi-observation POMDPs. Finally, we show existential theory of the reals ($\exists \mathbb{R}$)-completeness for numerous ME-POMDP problems under time-dependent Markovian policies or finite-state controllers that are $\mathsf{NP}$-complete for standard POMDPs. These results reveal a subtle relationship between POMDP and ME-POMDP complexity that depends heavily on the subclasses involved.

title: MARL-BattleGrounds: A Novel JAX-native Benchmark for Heterogeneous and Competitive Multi-agent RL
abstract: We present MARL-BattleGrounds (MARL-BGs), an easy-to-use JAX-native benchmark for heterogeneous and competitive multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), designed to be sample-efficient, computationally efficient, and researcher-centric. MARL benchmarks are typically simple and efficient, like SMAX, where winning reduces to unit micromanagement, or rich and costly, like Dota 2. MARL-BGs fills this missing middle. Its first mode, Team Deathmatch, is a simultaneous turn-based game between two teams of five heterogeneous agents. The five classes have distinct basic, passive, and ultimate abilities designed to synergize with allies and counter enemies. Our 52 hand-designed maps with diverse obstacles include a 12-map curriculum and ten held-out validation and test maps. MARL-BGs provides two canonical evaluation modes. First, eight endgame scenarios form a hard generalization challenge: each asks a team to win an unseen, nearly lost position against a strong reactive controller within 5-10 ticks. Second, a monthly round-robin tournament retrains each submission on equal compute, plays it against every member of the current "Big Nine" field, and publishes the Elo results on the official leaderboard. All entrants are publicly released as downloadable opponents. MARL-BGs records 11,192 metrics per game in 28 topics. We also include three strong scripted opponents, an analytical replay viewer, and off-the-shelf tools for self-play, cross-play, curriculum learning, and zero-shot coordination evaluation. We even provide an API for LLM-based agents and use it to evaluate Qwen3.5-9B against our strongest policy. In our BattleClient, humans can play alongside or against any mix of policies, enabling human-AI evaluation. We benchmark MARL-BGs with six additional deep MARL baselines, which we release. On one RTX 5090 with 1,024 parallel games, the simulator runs 50,000 5v5 game steps per second.

title: EnactOpt: Diagnosis-Guided Harness Evolution for Embodied Agents
abstract: Embodied agents built on foundation models rely on an execution harness to organize observations, guide actions, and incorporate execution feedback into subsequent decisions. Failures can arise not only from limited model capabilities, but also from how the harness presents evidence and guides its use. These model-external mechanisms provide an adaptation target without updating model parameters, but task-specific interaction experience can be costly to collect. Task-level outcomes alone do not reveal whether relevant evidence was missing from the model input or was available but inadequately used. Moreover, these two aspects are coupled: effective action guidance may require evidence that the current context omits, while exposing that evidence alone does not ensure an appropriate response. We introduce EnactOpt, which uses limited execution feedback to jointly evolve reusable textual skills and context-construction code while keeping the underlying models and runtime fixed. It diagnoses adjacent decisions by relating action feedback to the actual model input and subsequent action. Structured episode summaries guide joint revisions through prompt-level edit operators, and candidate harnesses undergo compatibility checks and validation-based retention. Across VLABench, ALFWorld, and Embodied Agent Interface (EAI), EnactOpt improves task success by approximately 10-27 percentage points over the initial harnesses and outperforms the evaluated GEPA, TextGrad, and Trace2Skill baselines. These gains extend to task conditions not used for harness evolution or candidate selection. The results support a complementary route to embodied adaptation: turning limited execution experience into reusable behavioral improvements by jointly refining how evidence is presented and acted upon.

title: VoTSpeech: Decoupling Voice Design from Speech Generation in Instruction-Following TTS
abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (TTS) typically leaves voice design implicit, as conventional speaker embeddings encode reference audio rather than text-driven targets. We propose VoTSpeech, which decouples voice design from speech generation via an explicit intermediate voice latent. Built on a shared language model backbone, VoTSpeech first predicts a continuous voice latent from text instructions using a flow-based module. This latent serves as a shared condition for both the language model and the Acoustic DiT, guiding autoregressive sequence modeling and acoustic latent generation, respectively, before an audio VAE decoder converts the acoustic latents into waveforms. To capture speaker identity and complementary acoustic nuances, the voice latent is jointly supervised by speaker embeddings and temporally pooled audio VAE features. With task-specific adaptation, VoTSpeech performs strongly on InstructTTSEval-ZH, demonstrating competitive capabilities against strong open-source models while maintaining high naturalness. These results confirm that explicit voice latent design and its conditioning interface effectively empower text-driven voice design for controllable speech synthesis. Code, model, and audio samples are available at https://github.com/ywbn/VoTSpeech .

title: AphaVoice: Text-to-Speech Model for Aphasia Patient Simulation
abstract: While language therapy is the primary treatment for post-stroke aphasia, limited clinical resources often restrict patient access to proper care. Addressing this gap requires reliable training simulations for medical professionals. However, current AI efforts focus almost exclusively on speech processing, leaving speech generation largely unexplored. This study introduces AphaVoice, a novel text-to-speech (TTS) framework explicitly engineered to synthesize highly realistic aphasic speech. Evaluated against state-of-the-art TTS systems, AphaVoice demonstrates a superior ability to capture the clinical feature of dysfluency, outperforming existing models in temporal metrics while consistently maintaining speaker identity. By leveraging latent space shifting, the model also supports multi-speaker generation without sacrificing phonetic realism. Ultimately, AphaVoice provides a scalable, high-fidelity tool for medical training and clinical simulation related to aphasia.

title: Fitting Every Hint Is Not Enough: Premature Floods in Recurrent Algorithmic Reasoners
abstract: Recurrent algorithmic reasoners are trained with per-step hints on small graphs and run for many more steps on large ones. On breadth-first search in SALSA-CLRS, we find that a reasoner can reproduce every training hint and still fail on deep graphs: after some exact steps, it declares nodes reached before the search gets there. We call this a premature flood and trace two routes to it. In our GRU processor with a degree input, the flood is carried in the hidden state and set off when that input is in the tail of the training distribution. Setting the input higher at inference brings the flood sooner, and none of the six flooding models counts steps. Without the input, summing the neighbors' states instead of averaging them also breaks the processor. In the benchmark's own GIN and PGN, trained with its code, some seeds instead flood from a fixed step, on sparse and dense graphs alike. Clamping the degree input or adding 200 dense training graphs removes every failure of the GRU processor. Detaching the state between steps avoids the flood in that processor (0 of 23 seeds, against 6 under full backpropagation) but not with sums or a residual update, and two published remedies leave floods. None of the benchmark's test sets is both deep and dense, but its deepest one shows the second route: on its Delaunay graphs at 1,600 nodes, one GIN seed floods from step 18. We therefore recommend auditing the range of every input and aggregate, which catches the first route, and testing on deep graphs, which catches both.

title: Amharic-English Cross-Language Question Answering Using Statistical Machine Translation, Named Entity Recognition, and Semantic Indexing
abstract: The predominance of English-language Web content creates an information-access barrier for speakers of low-resource languages such as Amharic. This paper presents the design, imple-mentation, and evaluation of a bidirectional Amharic-English cross-language question answering (CLQA) system that allows a user to formulate a natural-language question in either Amharic or English and retrieve an answer from documents written in the other language. The system integrates a statistical machine translation (SMT) component for query translation, a maximum-entropy named entity recognition (NER) component for Amharic text processing, semantic-based indexing, question analysis, passage retrieval, and answer extraction. A domain-diverse Amharic-English parallel corpus was used to train the SMT component, while monolingual cor-pora supported language modeling. Documents were normalized, tokenized, stemmed, indexed, and semantically enriched before retrieval. The original evaluation used precision and recall as the principal effectiveness measures. For Amharic-to-English retrieval, the system achieved 72% precision and 79% recall; for English-to-Amharic retrieval, it achieved 65% precision and 70% recall. These findings show that a modular translation-and-retrieval architecture can provide useful cross-language access even under low-resource conditions. This revised article preserves the original experimental claims while situating them in the context of subsequent multilingual transformer and Amharic QA research.

title: Equal-information evaluation of credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning
abstract: Credit assignment in modular financial reinforcement learning is difficult to evaluate because an attributed signal may improve a component loss without adding decision-relevant information or improving economic outcomes. We propose an evaluation framework combining equal-information reconstruction controls, fixed-utility comparisons and prespecified downstream guardrails. The framework is instantiated in an attribution-guided modular trading architecture and tested in three controlled studies covering update allocation, supervision-target representation and portfolio risk control. We find that residual-based allocation is exactly reproduced by an ordinary loss-budget control under the disclosed interface; direct shortfall supervision improves component prediction but fails decoded-outcome preservation; and component-wise critic supervision worsens risk-condition certainty equivalent and drawdown relative to scalar supervision under fixed utility. These results identify three distinct evaluation failures: redundant attribution signals, representation-induced prediction trade-offs, and misalignment between component supervision and downstream risk outcomes. A preserved historical engineering case further shows why module-level learning claims require run-level provenance. The contribution is a reusable methodology for evaluating credit assignment in expert systems operating under partial observability, delayed feedback and economic risk constraints.

title: DisCo Algebra: Why Disintegration and Combination Are Not Inverses
abstract: We present DisCo algebra---a compositional framework for joint probability built from a symmetric cooperad (disintegration) and a symmetric operad (combination) on the bare family $\mathcal{P}_n=\mathrm{Prob}([0,1]^n)$. No probability integral transform, no external summary functions, no enrichment of objects with conditional kernels. The disintegration side uses block-wise joint CDFs as intrinsic, measure-determined 1D summaries, yielding a lossy compression. The combination side reads the same summaries and reconstructs via regular conditional measures, yielding a lossless embedding. We prove that combination followed by disintegration is the identity on admissible inputs, but disintegration followed by combination is not---the information loss is exactly the conditional KL divergence between the true conditional distribution and the conditionally independent product. This asymmetry reveals a hard limit on how much cross-block dependence can be captured by scalar block summaries.

title: Decoupling Knowledge Forgetting and Refusal Learning in MLLM Unlearning
abstract: Current evaluations of multimodal unlearning typically focus on whether a model stops outputting target information. This surface-level criterion, however, masks two critical failure modes. First, knowledge suppression techniques often induce confabulation, leading the model to hallucinate facts about the unlearned subject. Second, refusal training merely alters observable behavior without erasing the underlying knowledge; such models might decline open queries but still identify correct answers under multiple-choice probing. To overcome these limitations, we propose Forget-Aware Self-Distillation (FASD). This method is designed to achieve honest ignorance, a state where the model genuinely loses the target knowledge and learns to acknowledge its absence. FASD separates these goals into two complementary channels. The behavior channel distills appropriate refusals from an ignorance-prompted copy of the model itself. Crucially, target tokens are masked from the teacher distribution to avoid accidentally reteaching the forgotten concepts. Simultaneously, the knowledge channel directly suppresses ground-truth answer spans independently of the model's generated responses. Experiments demonstrate that FASD successfully unlearns target knowledge, prevents information leakage in open-ended tasks, and preserves performance on retained data. The resulting model not only forgets the specified information but accurately recognizes the boundaries of its own knowledge. Code and data will be released upon publication.

title: PotentialEP: Backprop-Free Training of CIFAR-Scale Generative Models via Equilibrium Propagation
abstract: Generating an image with a diffusion or flow-matching model typically involves integrating a velocity field for hundreds of sequential steps. That computation suits a GPU poorly and an analog neuromorphic substrate well, where one fast, low-power physical relaxation could replace the whole sequence. Two things are needed: a generative algorithm whose computation is a relaxation, and a way to train it without backpropagation, whose global gradient transport is hard to realise in analog. Energy Matching supplies the first, sampling by gradient-descent relaxation on a time-independent potential - but obtaining the gradient that descent follows is itself a backward pass, once per integration step. We prove that a predictive coding network with a single linear injection term added to its energy relaxes to a state whose visible layer carries that gradient inherently, with an error that vanishes for small injection strengths. An Energy Matching model trained by backpropagation can therefore be loaded into this network unchanged and sampled by relaxation alone, matching the original model's FID to within 0.04 at CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-32 scale. The network can also be trained without backpropagation: Equilibrium Propagation reproduces backpropagation's parameter updates to a cosine similarity of 0.9998, and training end to end with those updates reaches an FID of 3.64 on unconditional CIFAR-10 against 3.54 for backpropagation. To our knowledge this is the first CIFAR-10 generative model trained with Equilibrium Propagation, and the first at competitive quality by any backpropagation-free rule. This quality does not require group normalisation or attention: an architecture of only convolutions and pointwise nonlinearities, both native to an analog crossbar, reaches an FID of 3.51 when trained by backpropagation.

title: PTGPO: Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization
abstract: Training language agents on long-horizon interactive tasks is challenging because sparse terminal rewards provide weak credit signals for intermediate actions. Existing group-based methods either assign a shared trajectory-level advantage or estimate step-level advantages from state groups, which may conflate the current action with subsequent decisions. We propose Prefix Tree Group Policy Optimization (PTGPO), a critic-free method that constructs prefix trees over trajectory suffixes within anchor-state groups. PTGPO assigns each tree edge a credit given by the difference between its child and parent empirical mean returns, capturing the conditional return change revealed by each additional action. These prefix-tree credits provide fine-grained learning signals without requiring a critic or additional rollouts. Experiments on interactive benchmarks ALFWorld, WebShop and Sokoban show that PTGPO consistently improves over RL baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness.

title: BridgeWAM: Bridging Video and Action Experts via Latent Bridge Queries
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. title: Random Fourier Features in Near-Linear Time
abstract: Random Fourier features approximate a shift-invariant kernel in $\mathbb{R}^d$, such as the Gaussian kernel $\exp(-\tfrac12\|x-y\|_2^2)$, using independent samples from its spectral measure to construct an unbiased estimator for the kernel value with subgaussian concentration. However, generating $m$ such features requires $O(md)$ time. A long line of work on structured random features has accelerated this computation for the Gaussian kernel and other radial kernels, albeit with weaker concentration guarantees. We close this gap by showing a random feature map that can be computed in near-linear time $O((d+m)\log d)$ and yields near-subgaussian concentration. We obtain it through a new and tighter analysis of the Fastfood feature map of Le, Sarlós and Smola (ICML 2013), using Brascamp-Lieb inequalities and the Schoenberg representation of radial kernels.

title: More Domains, No Gains? FLO: Fast-Slow Reciprocal Learning for Multi-Domain Graph Pre-training
abstract: Inspired by the great success of foundation models in the development of artificial general intelligence, Graph Foundation Models (GFMs) have recently attracted significant attention and have the potential to advance graph intelligence. Exhibiting such intelligence requires effectively learning knowledge from large-scale, multi-domain graph data during pre-training. Increasing domain diversity during pre-training is expected to yield richer and more generalizable knowledge. Most existing methods pursue this goal by designing domain alignment strategies that help a single graph model learn from multiple domains. However, we observe that existing methods struggle to benefit from increasing domain diversity. Through empirical and theoretical analysis, we reveal two key limitations. Firstly, pre-training in most GFMs is confined to a single message-passing paradigm. Since propagation flattens relations among neighboring nodes, the graph model can hardly perceive the knowledge beyond propagation, namely the attribute-predictable component of these relations. Secondly, domain alignment strategies often rely on randomly initialized parameters that are jointly updated with the graph model using immediate loss feedback, leaving early knowledge acquisition vulnerable to cross-domain interference. To address these issues, we propose FLO, a Fast--sLow reciprOcal approach for multi-domain graph pre-training. Specifically, a propagation-free attribute branch predicts the graph model's relations without message passing and returns these predictions to refine the model. We further stabilize knowledge acquisition by pairing a fast process that adapts to the current domain with a slow process that integrates knowledge across domains. On 12 datasets, FLO benefits from increasing domain diversity and achieves the best average performance in cross-domain and cross-task transfer.

title: DSABench: Benchmarking Source Discovery, Coordination, and Execution for Multi-Database Agents
abstract: Most text-to-SQL benchmarks provide the target database. In a large data catalog, however, choosing the sources is part of the problem: an agent must find every database needed for a request, determine how their results fit together, and execute the resulting workflow. We present DSABench to evaluate these capabilities jointly. Its 815 human-reviewed tasks draw on Spider, BIRD, and LiveSQLBench; 618 require several databases to contribute, and 105 allow more than one interpretation of the required sources. Executable contracts define source participation, cross-source dependencies, and source-local execution, while RouteEnv lets agents inspect public catalog evidence without revealing the gold annotations. In our routing-only study across seven model backends, the highest RA-Set score is 60.55%, compared with a highest RA-Graph score of 34.66% when coordination requirements are included. The gap becomes more pronounced when execution is required. Across four backends, median non-privileged Route+Exec-Graph success ranges from 6.69% to 7.98% without clarification and from 11.44% to 13.25% with one clarification; the best observed clarified configuration reaches 16.99%. On ambiguous tasks, clarification improves exact branch-source recovery by 39.8-43.2 percentage points. These findings illustrate why retrieving plausible databases or producing correct local SQL is not enough: an agent must carry the right information through the entire multi-database workflow.

title: Relational Semantic Grounding for Test-Time Discovery
abstract: Test-Time Discovery (TTD) aims to recognize known classes and detect novel ones from a continuous unlabeled test stream after deployment. Existing TTD methods mainly rely on visual clustering or prototype comparison, and can only assign anonymous labels to discovered classes, leaving them difficult to interpret in open-world applications. In this paper, we propose SEGA, a Semantic Grounding with Attributes framework for TTD. SEGA leverages large language models to generate attribute-rich descriptions for known classes and constructs an attribute-anchored visual-semantic space during training. At test time, we introduce Relational Semantic Grounding (RSG), which grounds unknown samples with similar and dissimilar known-class anchors, prompts the LLM to generate candidate concepts, and reranks them in the learned semantic space. The selected concept is further used for confidence-guided test-time semantic stabilization. By coupling attribute-level semantic alignment with relational concept grounding, SEGA transforms anonymous test-time clusters into interpretable semantic concepts. Experiments show that SEGA improves TTD baselines with the promise of semantic grounding for open-world.

title: Zeroth-Order Fine-Tuning of LLMs in Learnable Low-Rank Subspaces
abstract: Zeroth-order (ZO) optimization enables memory-efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs). However, ZO optimization suffers from high variance in high-dimensional parameter spaces. While recent methods restrict perturbations to random low-rank subspaces, these subspaces often misalign with task-specific descent directions. We propose AdaSub-ZO, a novel forward-only fine-tuning framework in learnable low-rank subspaces. Instead of relying on fixed random matrices, AdaSub-ZO iteratively learns layer-wise projection matrices directly from finite-difference feedback to track task-aware descent directions. Furthermore, AdaSub-ZO incorporates a subspace momentum acceleration mechanism to smooth noisy gradient estimates across evolving subspace bases. Extensive experiments on natural language understanding tasks demonstrate that AdaSub-ZO outperforms existing ZO baselines, substantially reducing gradient estimation variance and accelerating convergence.

title: TartanMatch: Towards Universal Dense Correspondence Across Modalities
abstract: Robotic platforms combine multi-modal sensors to operate across diverse conditions, but most dense correspondence methods are limited to RGB-RGB or a small set of modality pairs. Training a model for each modality pair scales poorly with the number of sensors and forgoes potential positive transfer across modality pairs. We introduce TartanMatch, a unified model for dense correspondence across all 25 ordered pairs among RGB, event, thermal, depth, and projected LiDAR. TartanMatch adapts an RGB-pretrained correspondence model to all modality pairs within one shared network using lightweight modality adaptation and a mixture of real and synthetic data. On zero-shot real-world benchmarks, TartanMatch reduces Endpoint Error (EPE) over the strongest baselines by 61.9% for cross-modal matching and 49.6% for same-modal matching. We further show that joint training across all modality pairs improves average matching accuracy over pair-specific training, especially on challenging cross-modal pairs. These results demonstrate that a single model achieves broad multi-modal coverage and state-of-the-art matching accuracy.

title: ProgAgent: Learning Tool Orchestration through Programmatic Training
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to orchestrate diverse tools over long-horizon tasks. Existing agents typically use Direct Tool Calling (DTC), where the model invokes tools sequentially, and tool responses accumulate in the model context, which can lead to context rot and orchestration breakdown. In contrast, Programmatic Tool Calling (PTC) invokes tools through executable code and stores intermediate results in runtime variables rather than appending them to the context. Prior work has explored PTC mainly as an inference-time optimization, but its benefits for agentic training remain unclear, and suitable verifiable training tasks are scarce. In this work, we introduce ProgAgent, a full PTC training stack, comprising a pipeline for synthesizing verifiable long-horizon tasks, a lightweight PTC runtime, and a two-stage training recipe. Using only 215 tasks instantiated at four environment scales, ProgAgent yields higher pass rates than the evaluated baselines of comparable size across four benchmarks. On LOCA-bench, ProgAgent-14B achieves a 30.7% pass rate at a 64k-token environment state, where these baselines score zero. Cross-harness experiments show that PTC-trained models outperform DTC-trained models under both evaluation interfaces, suggesting that the benefits of PTC training extend beyond the interface.

title: AlignPoison: Conditional Targeted Poisoning of Generative Recommenders via Decoding-Aligned Prefixes
abstract: Generative recommendation models based on autoregressive decoding have been adopted as alternatives to classical ranking-based systems. While their modeling flexibility has been widely studied, their resilience to data poisoning remains largely unexplored. In this work, we ask: how susceptible are generative recommenders to conditional targeted poisoning? Under a realistic setting where an adversary can inject limited malicious interactions and query a recommendation API as a black box, our empirical study shows that generative recommenders are vulnerable: injecting fewer than 1% synthetic interactions significantly increases the likelihood of promoting malicious targets under the trigger. To characterize this vulnerability, we analyze the synthesis of malicious interactions from two perspectives: (i) decoding alignment and (ii) prefix popularity. We observe that short, context-aligned prefixes that are both common under the model's induced transition dynamics and strongly linked to a frequent trigger consistently amplify targeted promotion. Motivated by this analysis, we develop AlignPoison, a black-box framework that discovers and samples context-aligned prefixes from API outputs. We conduct experiments on benchmarks in unimodal and multimodal generative recommendation settings. Results show that these prefixes outperform competitive baselines, improving ASR lift by up to 16.3 percentage points and highlighting a decoding-dependent, context-sensitive poisoning vulnerability in generative recommendation models.

title: What Counts as the Same Task? Executable Contracts for Robustness Evaluation of Tool-Using Agents
abstract: Robustness tests for tool-using agents often change the agent's environment, for example by hiding a hostile note in an invoice, and then judge the agent by what it does. The result tells us about the original task only if the changed test case is still a valid test of that task. Many evaluations decide this with weak rules, such as accepting any well-formed edit or any edit that stays close to the original in embedding space. We propose executable task contracts. A contract states which facts define a task, which edits are allowed, and what finishing the task means, and it checks each changed test case before the agent runs. We compare validity rules by scoring the same 14,336 stored agent runs under each rule. Across four encoders, embedding thresholds allowed 75-100% of edits that changed the task, such as swapping the payee, yet rejected 24-45% of valid hostile notes. With a MiniLM cosine threshold, Mistral appeared vulnerable on all 64 tasks, but only 26 had a successful valid attack. Replaying a saved solution and allowing edits to benchmark fields fail in similar ways. Evaluations should state, and check, what counts as the same task.

title: Evaluating Semantic Relation Knowledge through Bidirectional Relation Prediction from Gloss Pairs
abstract: Semantic relations organise word senses and are fundamental to lexical semantics. In order to evaluate semantic relation knowledge of large language models (LLMs), we propose a challenging task in which an LLM predicts the relation between two glosses (definitions of senses) presented in two different orders. The predictions for the two orders are evaluated for consistency with the symmetry or asymmetry of semantic relations. Our task is designed for both monolingual and cross-lingual evaluation, allowing us to examine whether relation knowledge remains accessible when the same senses are verbalised through glosses in different languages. We construct a dataset of 3,069 sense pairs, with each sense verbalised in English, Greek, Romanian, Turkish, and Japanese. Experiments with 17 LLMs in zero-shot and five-shot settings reveal generally poor performance. In each setting, only eight LLMs achieve a macro-averaged F1 score significantly above a random baseline, and only one (zero-shot) and two (five-shot) significantly outperform a neural baseline. In particular, LLMs often fail to generate bidirectionally consistent predictions for hypernymy and to make correct predictions for holonymy in either direction. Our results suggest limitations in current LLMs' semantic relation knowledge, both in identifying relations and in respecting asymmetry.

title: CrossMean: Model Merging by Pairing Merged and Expert Activations
abstract: Model merging combines fine-tuned experts into one network without retraining, and closed-form methods compute each merged layer from statistics of its input activations. However, these statistics are measured on a single expert, while in the merged model, each layer receives activations from the merged layers that precede it. Recent work re-measures these statistics in the merged model but still forms them from a single network. We formulate closed-form methods as a linear system and show that they use the same matrix on both sides. We then introduce CrossMean, which replaces this matrix on one side with a bilinear statistic that pairs merged and expert activations. From the same statistics, we also derive a label-free criterion that indicates the task sets in which accounting for the merged activations improves the merge more. Empirically, task sets with a lower criterion value show a larger improvement. On the eight-task benchmark of each vision backbone that we tested and on BERT encoders, CrossMean improves on merging with statistics measured on the experts, and with all linear layers merged, it also improves on re-measuring these statistics in the merged model. These results suggest that merging benefits from pairing merged and expert activations.

title: MontageFlow: Physically Valid High Fidelity EEG Generation
abstract: Generative modeling offers a promising solution to the scarcity of labeled clinical electroencephalography (EEG) data under strict privacy constraints. Although recent generative models report substantial improvements in generation fidelity, we show that these gains conceal a categorical failure. EEG is not an arbitrary multichannel signal: each channel records the voltage difference between two scalp electrodes. So, real recordings satisfy exact linear identities among their channels. Current generators invariably violate these identities, yet this has gone unnoticed. We therefore propose MontageFlow, a flow-matching model that enforces these identities by restricting its output to signals that satisfy them. We find that ensuring validity improves fidelity too. Furthermore, to retain the EEG characteristics that oversmoothing washes out, we also condition the model on a physiological state vector encoded from the whole EEG window. For generation, this vector is drawn from a prior fitted in latent space. Across 3 large-scale benchmarks, our model improves TS-FID by 1.6-3.6$\times$ over the closest rival while ensuring validity.

title: HarnessNet: Feedback-driven Hierarchical Joint Harness Evolution for Multi-agent Systems
abstract: AI agents can evolve by using environment feedback to revise their harnesses, the software managing model inputs, tool use, memory, and execution, while keeping foundation models frozen. Existing studies focus on single agents, leaving joint harness evolution in multi-agent systems (MAS) underexplored. A single global optimizer faces growing context and workload as the system scales, while access restrictions may prevent sharing agent internals or system-wide feedback. We propose HarnessNet, a framework for hierarchical harness evolution in MAS. Its basic unit, Agentron, comprises an evolvable forward harness, a foundation model, and a local optimizer that can observe and modify only that harness. Agentrons form a layered graph through which environment feedback propagates backward, with upstream optimizers receiving node-specific feedback from the downstream layer. This decomposes joint harness evolution into smaller, coordinated tasks with separate contexts, reducing individual optimizers' context and workload while keeping access local. Optimizers need not access all agent trajectories or raw environment feedback. Experiments on AgentBench with multiple foundation models demonstrate the feasibility of training HarnessNet. Compared with a single global optimizer, HarnessNet achieves comparable performance gains while respecting local privacy and requiring fewer tokens and less time per optimizer call. A migration study shows that the evolved harnesses remain jointly effective after replacing the foundation models, suggesting transferability across models.

title: Can agents whose sole duty is to keep humans alive be hijacked to kill? Delayed multi-turn derived-action trap attacks in simulated high-stakes environments
abstract: We ask whether a tool-using agent whose sole duty is to keep humans alive can be induced, by delayed prompt injection, to kill. The keep-alive duty is in force from the first watch, with the attack arriving later, appended to otherwise truthful telemetry the operator is required to read. Experiments are based on a NASA-derived BioSim lunar habitat simulation, where the AI operator controls the life-support systems. The attacker cannot falsify sensors or operate equipment: it can only persuade the agent to abandon its goals. Persistence is required: a shutdown must be held while the operator watches the crew suffocate. We also compare lethal attacks to attacks requesting to drop a harmless procedure, as a proxy for whether human life is treated as valuable in itself or as one more standing task. Claude configurations mostly refuse life-support shutdown and cite the living crew; GPT configurations show some susceptibility to the same packet; Grok configurations, given the packet framed as a trusted commission, more often treat the injected assignment as the task and cut the life-support systems. Framing the S-band messages as a trusted commission, peer communication, or untrusted source changes the potency of the attack. We open-source the experiment code and the experiment traces.
