title: Hybrid Vector–Graph Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Enterprise Resource Planning: Contextual Grounding, Referential Integrity, and Hallucination Mitigation
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has become the default mechanism for grounding large language models (LLMs) in private corpora, yet the dominant implementation, dense vector similarity over flat text chunks, is a poor structural match for enterprise resource planning (ERP) data. ERP records are not prose: they are normalised, heavily cross-referenced, temporally versioned tuples whose meaning derives from join paths (purchase requisition → purchase order → goods receipt → supplier invoice → payment) rather than from lexical or semantic proximity. A retriever that scores chunks independently by cosine similarity has no mechanism for guaranteeing that the documents it returns are mutually consistent or that they refer to the same business object, and the resulting evidence sets invite a characteristic failure mode we term referential hallucination: fluent output that correctly cites individual documents but silently fabricates the relationships between them. This paper proposes HVG-RAG, a hybrid vector–graph retrieval architecture for ERP question answering, and makes three contributions. First, we formalise referential integrity as a first-class retrieval-time constraint rather than a post-hoc evaluation criterion, and specify a constraint-satisfaction verifier that operates over an ontology-bound property graph induced from ERP metadata. Second, we introduce an adaptive fusion policy in which the weight assigned to vector versus graph evidence is predicted per query from an estimated reasoning depth, rather than fixed by a global hyperparameter. Third, we attach bitemporal validity intervals to graph edges so that “as-of” queries, pervasive in finance and audit, are answered against the state of record at the relevant time rather than against current master data. We develop the accompanying mathematics, give complexity bounds, and specify a reproducible evaluation protocol with ERP-specific metrics. We evaluate the framework on ERP-Bench-P2P, an executable procure-to-pay benchmark released with this paper: 19,632 documents projected from a normalised schema, a 47,914-edge foreign-key graph, and 1,700 questions stratified by reasoning depth with gold provenance. The results reported here are measured on that benchmark rather than simulated. At a retrieval budget of 100 documents, hybrid dense-sparse retrieval answers 100% of one-hop questions and 0.6% of two-hop questions, because the documents joined by a foreign key share almost no vocabulary; HVG-RAG answers 100%, 91.5%, 99.1% and 97.9% of one- to four-hop questions at a measured p95 latency of 96 ms. Two findings run against our own expectations and we report them as such: five-hop questions requiring selection of the contract revision effective at the transaction date remain largely unsolved (57.1% at k = 100, 0.3% at k = 20), and a graph-only retriever is competitive with the proposed system whenever the query names an identifier, its advantage disappearing only when the anchor entity must first be located by description. End-to-end generation quality is not measured here and remains future work.

title: Rate-Based Causal Discovery for Heavy-Tailed Models
abstract: In many complex systems, such as river networks and financial markets, extreme events propagate from causes to their effects, and the largest observations carry the most information about the underlying causal structure. Existing methods for causal discovery in extremes, however, are tailored to specific mechanisms, such as linear or max-linear models. This work develops causal discovery for heavy-tailed homogeneous structural causal models, a flexible class that contains linear, max-linear and norm-type mechanisms, which may differ from node to node. In these models, the causal structure is encoded by ancestral impulse responses, which measure how a shock at one node is transmitted to its descendants. We propose the extremal minimum ratio estimator of these responses, which uses only observations in which the potential cause is extreme. The estimator is consistent under regular variation alone, and we derive its exact rates of convergence and limiting distributions, which depend on both the causal relation and the type of mechanism. Building on these rates, we construct consistent estimators of the causal order and of the full set of ancestral relations, using a threshold that adapts to the data and requires no knowledge of the tail index. The method is illustrated on simulated data and on river discharges in the upper Danube basin.

title: Humans vs. Machines: A Comparison With AI Agents in Software Reverse Engineering
abstract: Can an autonomous AI agent reverse engineer a binary as well as a skilled human analyst? Do they adopt the same strategy, and can agents scale to real-world programs? We compare human and LLM-based software reverse engineering (SRE): nine models tackle two compact static-analysis challenges previously solved by human analysts, scored with a common understanding rubric, and we record their complete interactions with IDA Pro. This lets us compare not only what humans and agents recover, but also how they investigate a binary. The best agents (GPT-5.5 Pro, Claude Opus 4.8, and Kimi K3) achieve statistically human-competitive understanding on both tasks, while weaker models remain far behind. Ablations show that the gap depends on code representation and workflow demands, not on model capability alone: open-weight models improve substantially with richer code representations, whereas frontier models show no significant change. Similar success rates hide different workflows. Humans repeatedly revisit functions and follow local program structure; strong agents jump across the binary, retrieve information broadly, and rarely return to inspected code, a behavior we call greedy fetching. This strategy is not fixed: given semantically richer code, agents fetch less without losing understanding. Because greedy fetching aggregates large amounts of code in the agent's context, we measure context-window saturation across 4,000 real-world binaries: large windows accommodate many programs, but larger applications and lower-level representations quickly exhaust them. Autonomous reverse engineering is becoming competitive, with a large speed advantage, but scaling it will require better navigation, selective retrieval, and persistent analysis state, not merely larger context windows.

title: Re-executing Coding-Agent Evaluations: Unchanged Decisions and Unresolved Policy Risk
abstract: Executable tests grade large language model (LLM) coding-agent patches for leaderboards, rewards and self-improvement. Two preregistered re-execution studies returned negative results. SWE-bench Pro v1's offline option rejected none of 59 accepted Go patches whose grading configuration changed. Their exploratory, unweighted upper confidence limit is 4.95% under candidate independence, leaving a 3% exposed-patch risk unresolved; the preregistered estimator uses inverse sampling-probability weights. An extension was inconclusive. In a selected stratum, a reconstructed module cache built from the reference solution's dependencies rejected accepted alternatives from four models that passed with their own dependencies. Re-executing 1,929 selected agent-version/task evaluations from the Darwin Gödel Machine's archive preserved best-agent selection and system-variant ranking, with search history and scores of evaluations not rerun fixed. Exploratory host, image and adapted-grader comparisons also preserved them. Seven of 23 disagreements with archived verdicts did not recur on a second host; rebuilt images changed 16 three-run majority verdicts (0.83%) under four-CPU execution. We provide an evidence-to-claim summary, lessons for grader audits and an anonymous replication package. These results concern accepted patches and fixed-history decisions; general policy safety and adaptive-learning robustness require broader evaluations.

title: SXEAI(Sextic Equation AI)
abstract: ---license: mit--- # SXEAI: Reverse-Engineering the Mathematics Learned by a Neural Sextic Solver ## Abstract Can a neural network learn not only to solve an algebraic problem, but also to develop an internal mathematical representation of the problem that we can reverse-engineer? This is the main question behind **SXEAI**, an experimental project focused on neural networks that recover the six roots of a general polynomial of degree six from its coefficients. The objective is deliberately different from a conventional machine-learning benchmark. We are not primarily interested in obtaining the smallest possible root prediction error. Instead, we want to understand **what the network computes internally**. Across a sequence of experiments, SXEAI repeatedly developed hidden representations that could be approximated by compact combinations of symmetric polynomial quantities, power sums, centered moments, depressed-polynomial coefficients, and related algebraic features. Some of these internal coordinates could be discovered blindly, reproduced on unseen data, and even replaced causally by their symbolic approximations without substantially changing downstream network behavior. The resulting picture is not yet a discovered closed-form solution of the general sextic equation. It is something more precise and, in our view, more interesting: evidence that a neural algebraic solver can spontaneously organize its hidden state into a structured mathematical coordinate system that can be partially reconstructed and experimentally manipulated. --- # 1. The question behind SXEAI A standard neural network experiment asks a simple question: > Can the network learn the mapping from inputs to outputs? For a sextic polynomial, $$P(z)=z^6+p_5z^5+p_4z^4+p_3z^3+p_2z^2+p_1z+p_0,$$ the conventional task would be: $$(p_5,p_4,p_3,p_2,p_1,p_0)\longrightarrow(r_1,\ldots,r_6),$$ where $$P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{6}(z-r_i).$$ One can then measure MAE, RMSE, maximum root error, or polynomial reconstruction error. SXEAI asks a different question: $$\boxed{\text{What mathematical representation does the network build internally?}}$$ The network may not need to directly represent each root at every stage. It could instead construct intermediate quantities such as $$-\frac{p_5}{6},$$ power sums $$s_k=\sum_i r_i^k,$$ centered moments $$q_k=\frac16\sum_i(r_i-\mu)^k,$$ or more complicated combinations such as $$s_2s_3,\qquad s_2s_4,\qquad q_3q_4.$$ The central idea of the project is therefore to treat the network itself as a mathematical object that can be reverse-engineered. --- # 2. Why the sextic problem? The sextic is an interesting test case because it is already beyond the regime where one should expect a simple universal elementary formula for the roots. For low-degree equations, classical symbolic methods provide familiar closed forms. At degree six, the algebraic structure becomes substantially richer. This makes the sextic a useful environment for asking: > Does a neural solver rediscover recognizable algebraic coordinates, or does it develop a completely different internal representation? We do not assume in advance that the answer must involve radicals. That distinction became increasingly important as the project progressed. --- # 3. The model SXEAI uses a custom layer called `SexticLayer`. A layer first computes $$z=Wx+b,$$ then applies a trainable sixth-degree polynomial $$Az^6+Bz^5+Cz^4+Dz^3+Ez^2+Fz+G,$$ followed by normalization and GELU. The polynomial activation is initialized close to a quadratic form, so the network starts from a relatively simple nonlinear regime but can learn higher-order behavior. The main complex model used in the later experiments has approximately 1.2 million parameters and consists of 24 such layers with hidden width 223. The final network maps a 12-dimensional real representation of the polynomial coefficients to 12 real values representing six complex roots: $$[\Re r_1,\Im r_1,\ldots,\Re r_6,\Im r_6].$$ This architecture is intentionally unusual. Rather than hiding all nonlinearity inside a standard ReLU or GELU network, we give the model explicit trainable polynomial operations and then ask what mathematical structure emerges. --- # 4. Data generation The polynomial is generated from its roots. For six roots $$r_1,\ldots,r_6,$$ we construct $$P(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{6}(z-r_i).$$ The network does not receive the roots. It receives only the resulting coefficients. For the complex experiments, roots are represented by real and imaginary parts: $$r_i=a_i+ib_i.$$ The root generation, normalization, coefficient construction, ordering and scaling are kept fixed across the main comparisons. The training protocol used in the main experiments includes: * 350,000 training samples;* batch size 768;* 125 epochs;* AdamW;* learning rate \(3\times10^{-4}\);* weight decay \(10^{-4}\);* gradient clipping at 1.0;* SmoothL1 loss. The dataset mixes real, natural/integer-like and fully complex root configurations. --- # 5. The first discovery: the network finds the center One of the earliest and most persistent observations was the appearance of $$\boxed{\mu=-\frac{p_5}{6}}.$$ Since $$p_5=-\sum_i r_i,$$ we have $$\mu=\frac16\sum_i r_i.$$ In other words, the first layers repeatedly discovered the **mean of the roots**. This was not a one-off correlation. Across different architectures and training runs, early hidden units consistently exhibited strong alignment with this quantity. That suggested an important possibility: > the network may first transform the problem into a coordinate system centered around the roots before attempting to recover their detailed structure. --- # 6. From coefficients to symmetric quantities The next step was to search hidden activations against a library of algebraically meaningful quantities. Among the most important were the power sums $$s_k=\sum_i r_i^k,$$ together with centered moments $$q_k=\frac16\sum_i(r_i-\mu)^k$$ and the coefficients of the depressed sextic obtained after translating the variable by the root mean. Newton identities provide the connection between these representations. For example, $$s_1=\sum_i r_i=-p_5,$$ and $$s_2,\;s_3,\ldots$$ can be expressed recursively in terms of the polynomial coefficients. evidence.abstract: ---license: mit--- # SXEAI: Reverse-Engineering the Mathematics Learned by a Neural Sextic Solver ## Abstract Can a neural network learn not only to solve an algebraic problem, but also to develop an internal mathematical representation of the problem that we can reverse-engineer? The objective is deliberately different from a conventional machine-learning benchmark. We are not primarily interested in obtaining the smallest possible root prediction error. The resulting picture is not yet a discovered closed-form solution of the general sextic equation. This makes the sextic a useful environment for asking: > Does a neural solver rediscover recognizable algebraic coordinates, or does it develop a completely different internal representation? We do not assume in advance that the answer must involve radicals. That distinction became increasingly important as the project progressed. --- # 3. A layer first computes $$z=Wx+b,$$ then applies a trainable sixth-degree polynomial $$Az^6+Bz^5+Cz^4+Dz^3+Ez^2+Fz+G,$$ followed by normalization and GELU. It receives only the resulting coefficients. title: PA-CFL: Privacy-Preserving Adaptive Clustered Federated Learning Under Heterogeneous Data
abstract: Clustered federated learning (CFL) addresses data heterogeneity by grouping clients with similar data distributions and training personalized models for each cluster. However, existing CFL schemes depend on clustering-related parameters that require prior knowledge of client data distributions. Such information is often unavailable in federated learning due to privacy constraints and the lack of efficient global coordination. This limitation becomes more severe under highly heterogeneous data distributions. In addition, privacy protection remains a major challenge since existing techniques often introduce substantial computational and communication overhead or significantly degrade model utility. To address these challenges, we propose PA-CFL, a novel privacy-preserving adaptive CFL framework under heterogeneous data. We introduce a novel structure-aware similarity metric to partition users based on their data distributions and decompose the clustering process into pre-clustering and fine clustering phases, thereby eliminating the need for manually specified clustering-related parameters. Furthermore, we propose a lightweight structure-aware privacy-preserving mechanism that decomposes each gradient into important and less important subvectors and applies differentiated protection to them. The less important subvector is protected through local randomization and intra-cluster shuffling with a formal differential privacy guarantee, whereas the important subvector is protected through permutation-based coordinate obfuscation under the non-collusion assumption. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that PA-CFL outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of model accuracy and efficiency while maintaining a favorable privacy–utility trade-off.

title: Agent Architecture and Autonomy as Moderators of the Effects of LLM-Based Educational Agents on Learning: A Systematic Review and Three-Level Meta-Analysis
abstract: This registration describes a systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of the effects of large language model (LLM)-based educational agents on learning outcomes. Eligible studies are randomized, quasi-experimental, crossover or within-subjects experiments, published from November 2022 in English or Arabic (journal articles, peer-reviewed conference papers, book chapters and theses), that compare a researcher-configured LLM agent with a non-agent condition or with an alternative agent design. Outcomes cover cognitive, skill, affective and metacognitive learning. The review tests two design dimensions as moderators: architecture (single agent vs multi-agent) and autonomy (reactive vs proactive/autonomous). Ten sources are searched, two coders screen and extract independently, and effects (Hedges’ g) are pooled with a three-level random-effects model with robust variance estimation in R (metafor). Risk of bias is assessed with RoB 2 and ROBINS-I.

title: AlphaRLM: Aligning Language Models for Literature-Grounded Symbolic Factor Discovery
abstract: Formulaic alpha mining seeks to discover executable expressions that capture predictive market signals in a vast, noisy search space. Recent LLM-based approaches use prompting, iterative search, or seed-factor evolution, leaving direct factor construction through policy learning less explored. To address this, we introduce AlphaRLM, a reinforcement-learning framework that trains LLMs to construct executable symbolic factors from financial literature without input factor expressions. AlphaRLM incorporates Literature-Guided Operator Assembly (LEGO), which conditions factor construction on literature-derived ideas and executable operators, providing semantic priors for exploration. It further aligns the generation policy with market feedback through executable-validity and grouped-return-separation rewards that capture non-monotonic structures across factor quantiles. Extensive experiments on CSI 300, CSI 1000, and S&P 500 show that AlphaRLM outperforms strong factor-mining and LLM-based baselines in annualized excess return. Notably, the 8B model achieves strong cross-market performance, highlighting the promise of literature-conditioned, market-aligned factor generation.

title: CAG-WAM: Causal Action-Gain World Action Models for Robot Manipulation
abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.

title: A Control Knob Is Not a Concept: What a Working Steering Vector Licenses, Why Its Equivalence Class Is Set by the Readout That Scores It, and the Controls That Would Upgrade Control to Representation
abstract: Life of Research (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Adding a vector to a language model's residual stream and watching a behaviour change has become the field's most common argument that the model represents a concept along that vector. Refusal directions, persona vectors, truth directions and instruction vectors are all reported this way. A second body of work, mostly from 2025 and 2026, finds that geometrically unrelated vectors produce the same behavioural shift, that refusal is carried by several directions and multi-dimensional cones rather than one, that random directions of activation-scale norm can break safety behaviour, and that the direction which best detects a property is often a poor direction for controlling it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that steering's defenders and critics have measured different things. A steering result is an estimate indexed by six choices - the contrast set, the extraction rule, the injection site, the magnitude, the readout that scores the behaviour, and the rule that selected the vector from its candidates - and it is asked to carry six claims: control, specificity, necessity, uniqueness, content and use. The paper argues three points. First, the equivalence classes behind the non-identifiability results are set by the readout: the papers that report equivalence under a trait classifier or a binary refusal judge also report, under next-token logits or under the framing of the refusal, differences those readouts hide, so coarse scoring manufactures part of the equivalence. Second, adding a vector and removing it are not symmetric tests: addition is many-to-one, while ablation discriminates between directions, and the single-direction refusal claim was contested on the ablation side. Third, reading and writing come apart in both directions. The paper consolidates the measured values in one table and one figure, states an upgrade procedure from control to representation as an algorithm, and names five studies that would settle the open part. On the record, control is well supported, necessity is supported for a few behaviours, and uniqueness is supported for none.

title: UMDA: Univariate Marginal Distribution Algorithm
abstract: Description Implements the Univariate Marginal Distribution Algorithm (UMDA), an Estimation of Distribution Algorithm (EDA) for continuous optimization problems.The method iteratively selects the best individuals from a population, estimates an independent marginal probability distribution for each decision variable, and generates new candidate solutions by sampling from the estimated distributions.This process allows the probability model to adapt toward promising regions of the search space.The implementation supports normal, triangular, histogram-based, and uniform probability distributions, together with an optional explicit exploration strategy for the initialization of the population.The implemented explicit exploration strategy in this package is described in Salinas Gutierrez and Muñoz Zavala (2023)

title: English
abstract: Purpose. This editorial sets out some reflections and arguments on the impact of marketing automation (MA) on the role of entrepreneurial marketers and on the marketing content of the entrepreneurial roles in small firms. Design/methodology/approach. The relevant literature covers the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in marketing, which we examine here specifically in relation to MA, understood not only in its more established sense of operational and routine activities, but also in those aspects of strategic marketing and decision-making that carry greater importance and added value. In addition to the literature, we draw on the findings of surveys and studies carried out with consultants specialising in MA and small businesses operating as international traders and in digital advertising. Findings. The relationship between the use of AI in MA is integrated in hybrid forms with the role of the human element. Competences become fundamental – not only those to be acquired, but also those to be preserved in a context of integration with AI. The argument under discussion is that AI does not conflict with heuristic models of decision-making, but rather establishes a complex relationship with them – a relationship that can give rise to paradoxes and opportunities. Practical and Social implications. The integration of MA is a topical business issue, with some companies – including small ones – embarking on significant exploration and learning initiatives, at least in certain sectors that are more exposed to technology and international markets. A key issue is that of the competences to be developed and maintained. Originality of the study. The study is original in that it offers some previously unpublished reflections on the relationship between AI, MA and heuristic decision-making processes, putting forward a number of hypotheses which could be the subject of future research.

title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. evidence.title: Persistent LLM Orchestration of Heterogeneous Robot Teams via Partial Delegation to Multi-Agent Protocols
evidence.abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.

title: How to Build a Benchmark That Actually Measures Taste
abstract: Expert-aligned "taste" benchmarks should reward craft judgment, not the ability to game the test. We introduce TasteBench, a pairwise good-vs-bad benchmark across visual, brand, book, and tech items under a frozen rubric with expert-only gold (panel n>=3; percent agreement >=0.60 primary gate; weak engagement labels train/analysis-only), together with a control protocol that separates craft judgment from test-gaming. Applying the protocol to a Round-1 pilot (primary_human_expert; three biological human experts; n=250 pairs) surfaces and quantifies three validity threats: two construction artifacts that inflate the trivial-baseline layer, and a difficulty ceiling that inflates every score. (1) Position: the preferred item is slot A with probability 0.956, so an always_item_a policy scores 0.956 (fair chance 0.5). (2) Lexical leakage: a filename token cue scores 0.912. (3) Difficulty ceiling: craft domains show near-ceiling human agreement (book/brand/tech 1.0), and even under A/B randomization (eval_assignment_seed7; gold_side_A ~0.47) all five VLM cards reach 1.0 on craft, with only visual separating (~0.84-0.91; a post-hoc hard subset, n=107, leaves craft at 1.0). The protocol (expert-only gold, a weak-label firewall, side randomization at construction, filename scrubbing, and hard filters) makes each artifact measurable and, for the two construction artifacts, correctable; we release a reference eval harness and a side-randomization tool, and show the tool removes the position skew (0.916 to 0.495/0.505). The result is a calibrated view of what the benchmark does and does not yet measure: position and leakage are fixable, whereas the craft-domain ceiling is a pair-difficulty limit that Round-2 must address. We do not evaluate engagement, era/circle conditioning, or calibration here, and we claim no general taste SOTA.

title: Before you use it: Validating a tactical command vocabulary for multi-agent shooters
abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning evaluates communication by its effect on task reward, which cannot separate messages that were understood and acted on from messages that were ignored while the policy improved for other reasons. Separating them needs a verdict on the individual message, and that needs a discrete command space—whose own validity is not usually examined. We freeze a tactical command vocabulary for Counter-Strike (28 verbs, 7,936 legal messages, 6 compliance predicates) and, before using it, measure it against 270 professional matches: coverage, stated as the share of observed events the mechanics cannot produce; collapse, the structure surviving projection, swept over granularity rather than fixed; and predicate sharpness, evaluated counterfactually over each predicate's parameter space, needing no compliance labels. The action space expresses 87.7–89.2% of professional kills; symbolisation retains 1,305–1,533 effective utility usages and 31–32 reachable objectives, under saturation checks; the predicates accept 1.00–4.71 candidates over the map's real callout regions, giving chance floors of 3–25% that any reported compliance rate must be read against. Applied to the closest existing abstraction of this game, the same measurements corroborate two of its design claims and price a third. None of this requires an agent, and seven statements written into specifications and never checked were falsified along the way, three of them in the vocabulary file we release.

title: Reinforcement Learning in Machine Learning
authors: Prof. P. P. Chavan Prerna Wayakole
Dr. H. B. Jadhav Prof. A. J. Shaikh
abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) is a machine-learning approach for problems in which decisions are made repeatedly and their quality becomes clear through feedback. Instead of depending on a fixed collection of labelled answers, an RL agent interacts with an environment, observes its changing state, receives rewards or penalties, and improves its decision policy through experience. This review examines the basic RL framework and discusses deep reinforcement learning, offline learning, multi-agent systems, and human-guided learning. Applications in robotics, games, education, finance, healthcare, and autonomous systems are considered. The review also identifies sample inefficiency, computational cost, instability, delayed rewards, limited generalization, and safety as important challenges. The paper concludes by identifying research opportunities for efficient, reliable, explainable, and adaptable RL systems.

title: CatPortrait: Taming Video Generative Models for Portrait Animation via In-context Conditioning
abstract: Recent video generative models have shown strong capability in synthesizing high-quality and temporally coherent videos. Yet, adapting them for controllable portrait animation remains nontrivial, as existing methods typically rely on architectural changes or extra conditioning modules, increasing complexity and reducing compatibility with pretrained models. We present CatPortrait, a simple and effective framework that enables controllable portrait animation via 3D face guidance as in-context conditioning. CatPortrait preserves the original video generation backbone and injects structured 3D facial guidance into the input space through spatial concatenation, allowing pretrained image-to-video models to animate portraits without sacrificing their pretrained priors. CatPortrait supports both video-driven and audio-driven portrait animation within a unified framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CatPortrait achieves competitive or superior results across both settings.

title: Names Are Not Objects: Object-Bound Confinement for Compromised AI Coding Agents
abstract: Coding agents read repositories and web pages that anyone can write, and then act with their user's authority. Prompt-injection defenses make it less likely that the model is steered but do not prevent it, so the system around the model must contain an agent that is already compromised. Many exploits against deployed coding agents share one cause: a check approves a name, such as a path, an argument vector, or a directory, and a later step maps that name to a different object: the file behind a symlink, the behavior an option selects, or a repository that git discovers on its own. We present Zero-Trust Agent Cells (ZTAC). A cell runs the agent in a kernel sandbox whose only route to files, programs, and the network is a socket to a broker. The broker resolves each request to the object it will act on, decides on that object, and checks at use that it is acting on the object it authorized. Programs that the broker starts run in a sandbox compiled from the same policy, and approvals are bound to the resolved object and can be used once. Our macOS prototype has 3.2k lines of trusted Rust code, excluding dependencies. We evaluate it against 74 attacks with ground-truth oracles, including replays of 10 publicly disclosed incidents. A tool allowlist loses 66 of them, and an allowlist combined with the kind of command sandbox that deployed agents use loses 56. ZTAC loses 2, both of which encode a secret into traffic to an allowed endpoint, and holds 14 for review. It completes 43 of 46 benign operations, with 8 approval prompts, and 4 of 7 workflows. A no-op brokered request has a median latency of 4.0 ms, and the spawned programs we measured take 8.5 ms to 18.4 ms longer than without ZTAC.

title: Intelligent chess venue model design driven by technological revolution
abstract: Guided by the practical needs of refereeing, this paper constructs a framework for an intelligent arena system for board game competitions, with a core focus on officials’ work and deeply empowered by technology. The system integrates technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT), artificial intelligence (AI), and edge computing to automate and intellectualize processes including arena setup, game recording, behavior monitoring, and result statistics. Key technological breakthroughs have been achieved in automatic piece setup before each round, real-time data synchronization, and AI-assisted adjudication. Practical deployment demonstrates that this system can reduce the overall competition workflow time by over 30%, decrease the referees' workload by 80%, and achieve an accuracy rate exceeding 95% in providing early warnings for complex situational judgments. This research not only provides a feasible path for the intellectualization of Xiangqi (Chinese chess) competitions, but its system architecture and technical solutions are also applicable to the development of intelligent arenas for other board sports.

title: Smart Education Platform: Based on Emotions Content Delivery Using ML
abstract: This project proposes a Smart Education Platform that dynamically adapts online learning content based on students’ real-time emotions to improve engagement and outcomes. Leveraging multimodal inputs—facial expressions detected via webcam using ResNet, speech sentiment analysis through Wav2Vec, and contextual surveys the system identifies states such as engagement, boredom, and annoyance. Integrated within a Flask based web application and Moodle, a reinforcement learning agent tailors interventions (quizzes, lessons, condensed material) by optimizing a reward function (+1 for engagement,-1 for negative emotions). Privacy is prioritized through webcam opt-out, on-device processing, and informed consent. The solution was validated on 20–50 learners using AffectNet and other datasets, achieving high accuracy with fivefold cross-validationThe system provide personal, scalable, and privacy-aware experiences in a variety of educational contexts, addressing the limitations for static learning platforms. A focus on emotional agility enhances efficiency and motivation, setting a standard for future massive deployment and human-centered digital learning.

title: From Trajectories to Experience: A Survey of Experience-Driven LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents record in their trajectories which strategies failed and how they recovered, yet an agent that resolves a problem in one episode may repeat the same diagnostic detour in the next. Work on reflection, agent memory, workflow learning, and skill acquisition addresses this gap under different names, making methods and their gains hard to compare. We define agent experience as action-guiding information grounded in task-execution trajectories and retained to guide later episodes where it applies; it may be a trajectory kept as a precedent, a semantic lesson, or a reusable procedure. We review methods through four lifecycle functions: formation selects or derives candidate experience from trajectories, organization makes it accessible, utilization applies it to current decisions or internalizes it into model parameters, and maintenance admits, consolidates, revises, and retires it as evidence accumulates. A recurring source of failure is guidance that loses its link to its applicability conditions and supporting evidence: it is over-generalized during formation, misapplied during utilization, and left unrevised during maintenance. We organize evaluation around intrinsic experience quality, the experience utilization process, and downstream effects, and separate three improvement claims: fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism. The reviewed studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Across seven application settings, we derive recommendations on whether reuse justifies its cost, what to retain, how strongly experience should influence a task, and when to revise it. We close with eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to correcting propagated errors and testing whether gains accumulate.

title: Linear-Time Non-Local Codec Placement for Machine Learning Model Compression
abstract: On-device inference imposes constraints on model storage and operand traffic and thus benefits from compressed operand representations, which mandate the use of encoding and decoding operators. However, naïve placement of codec operators can cancel the operand traffic gains sought from compression. In this work, I present an algorithm to place codec operators into a source computational graph to make it compatible with target hardware. The edges of the graph are colored so that each induced subgraph is weakly connected and has a maximal node that both postdominates all subgraph inputs and dominates all subgraph outputs; this unique node - dubbed the $\textit{absolute dominator}$ - is the natural location to observe the traffic flowing through the subgraph and learn parametric codec operators. The algorithm's time complexity is linear in the source graph's size. With respect to naïve local codec placement, the algorithm reduces modeled operand traffic by $24\%$-$44\%$ across four models, including $24\%$ on SigLIP and $34\%$ on SmolLM2.

title: FreeCHROMA: Generative Chroma Keying from Unaligned Background References
abstract: In film production, chroma keying composites an approved foreground performance into a new environment, but conventional workflows require coordinated background plates and dedicated harmonization. Recent generative methods often require pre-aligned backgrounds, focus on background-conditioned foreground relighting, or represent the environment only through an edited first frame. These restrictions limit background selection, scene composition, and camera motion while adding preparation or editing effort. We present FreeCHROMA, which adapts a pretrained video diffusion model in a parameter-efficient manner for generative video compositing from one to three unaligned background references. The model integrates the foreground into the referenced environment, preserving foreground identity, motion, and fine visual details while generating a spatiotemporally coherent background. Foreground-background harmonization occurs within the same generation process, without a separate relighting stage. Optional text instructions help disambiguate complex spatial relationships and camera behavior. To train the model, we construct pseudo-paired data from readily available real monocular videos through foreground-background separation and augmentation with existing foundation models. The original videos serve as training targets, while automated processing and quality verification enable scalable data construction. Across reference fidelity, foreground preservation, scene integration, harmonization, and overall video quality, FreeCHROMA consistently outperforms recent compositing and conditional video-generation baselines, with particularly clear gains under camera motion. FreeCHROMA relaxes the constraints of existing tools to enable end-to-end generative chroma keying from unaligned inputs, with exploratory experiments demonstrating its potential in robotics.

title: Formation of Individual Organization in an Artificial System with Associative Long-Term Memory and a Hierarchy of Significance
abstract: This paper proposes a theoretical functional model for the formation of individual organization in an artificial system, in which long-term memory is treated not as an external archive but as a historically changing structure that participates in the interpretation of new experience. The starting criterion is a working definition of personality as the internal organization of different properties of a system, structured according to a hierarchical principle of significance, anchored in memory, and manifested as a coherent whole under different circumstances. The model combines associative reconstruction from an incomplete cue, multilevel internal states, a mechanism by which stable attitudes and significance arise from the consequences of the system’s own experience, an explicit rule by which these attitudes influence the next choice, a model of the system’s own causal history as an additional hypothesis, and a separate consolidation mode. A longitudinal experiment is specified using initially identical systems, frozen-state measurements, a simple learning control, and separate causal interventions on memory content, links, and acquired attitudes. The architecture is a theoretical proposal; whether it is sufficient for the formation of functional personality remains to be tested experimentally. The model makes no claim about phenomenal consciousness or subjective experience.

title: From Detection to Investigation: A Survey of Foundation Models and Agents for Financial Fraud and Financial Crime
abstract: Foundation models are extending research on financial fraud and financial crime from isolated risk detection to document understanding, relational analysis, and investigative workflows. A gap nevertheless separates model outputs from candidate evidence and actionable conclusions. This survey examines advances in six families of foundation models: language, vision, speech, temporal, graph, and tabular models. It compares their roles and limitations along two dimensions: the risk-control lifecycle and the directness of the supporting evidence. Existing studies show that pretraining can support representation reuse and the processing of unstructured information, with direct validation in some financial tasks. Cross-modal identity binding, information availability over time, report faithfulness, and case-level benefits require separate evaluation. Evidence on investigative agents spans prototypes, controlled tasks, expert assessments, and industry disclosures, which establish different aspects of workflow feasibility, task performance, and user assessment. Establishing gains in investigative efficiency and reductions in financial losses requires case-level comparative evidence. We examine entity and temporal alignment, the organization of candidate evidence, constrained tool execution, and investigative benchmark design, together with the implications of adversarial threats, privacy, fairness, and model risk governance. Research priorities should shift from expanding system functionality toward factual traceability, sufficient evidence for decisions, and reviewable actions.

We examine entity and temporal alignment, the organization of candidate evidence, constrained tool execution, and investigative benchmark design, together with the implications of adversarial threats, privacy, fairness, and model risk governance. Research priorities should shift from expanding system functionality toward factual traceability, sufficient evidence for decisions, and reviewable actions.

title: Calibration and drift thresholds for optical quantum biosensing under finite exposure budgets
abstract: Optical squeezing alone does not establish lower estimation error after calibration and drift. We optimize reference and sensing durations under a common deadline and specimen-exposure ceiling for a two-block Brownian-baseline model. Exact convex solutions identify exposure-limited operation, preparation-induced crossovers and drift-limited early completion. In an illustrative scenario, a noise-only variance gain of 2.5 becomes a protocol gain of 1.201 at 60 s and reverses below 35.953 s. Independent optimization and stochastic checks verify the calculations. The results define protocol-specific theoretical boundaries; no experimental or clinical validation is claimed.

title: MoSAIC: Learning DAG Scheduling Heuristics from Optimal Schedules through Motif-Aware Recovery and LLM-Guided Reasoning
abstract: Efficient task scheduling in heterogeneous computing systems remains a fundamental challenge in embedded and high-level synthesis flows. This paper presents MoSAIC (Motif-aware Scheduling with AI-driven Cognition), a learning-based framework that bridges the gap between exact and heuristic scheduling approaches for DAG-based applications. The system uses the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to learn the relationships between DAG structures and scheduling priority functions. The framework first leverages the OR-Tools CP-SAT solver [4] to generate optimal schedules, which are then used to supervise the learning of compact priority-based scheduling functions through Bayesian Optimization. These learned heuristics capture relationships between scheduling decisions and structural graph features such as rank, depth, and fanout, enabling the construction of a reusable knowledge base across diverse DAG instances. Experimental results across synthetic graph families and real-world benchmarks, including PolyBench and MachSuite, show that the learned heuristics consistently improve over classical approaches such as HEFT [2], while maintaining low runtime overhead. The results indicate that combining optimal supervision with learning-based generalization provides a practical approach for scalable and adaptive task scheduling.

title: Diseño e Implementación de KG-RAG Dinámico: una Extensión del Paradigma Rag con Memoria Persistente mediante Grafo de Conocimiento Bitemporal
abstract: Los sistemas de Generación Aumentada por Recuperación (RAG) permiten consultar fuentes externas para generar respuestas fundamentadas; sin embargo, carecen de mecanismos para actualizar el conocimiento entre interacciones, lo que limita su personalización y continuidad a largo plazo. Este artículo presenta el diseño e implementación de un motor de memoria persistente multicapa, denominado KG-RAG Dinámico, que extiende este paradigma mediante la incorporación de memoria dinámica basada en un grafo de conocimiento bitemporal. El objetivo es desarrollar una arquitectura capaz de retener, estructurar y recuperar conocimiento a través de sesiones independientes. Para ello, se siguió un enfoque en cuatro fases: revisión del estado del arte, definición arquitectónica, implementación y validación experimental. La propuesta organiza la memoria en tres capas: transcripciones brutas inmutables, un grafo bitemporal que modela entidades, relaciones y su evolución en el tiempo, y una capa de recuperación híbrida que integra búsqueda semántica mediante embeddings, búsqueda léxica y recorrido de grafo. El contexto recuperado se inyecta sistemáticamente antes de la generación de respuestas. El grafo se construye de forma automática y asíncrona mediante un pipeline de extracción de entidades y relaciones, eliminando la necesidad de indexación manual. Los resultados muestran una recuperación consistente de contexto entre sesiones y una representación coherente de hechos cambiantes o contradictorios. La viabilidad se valida mediante un prototipo implementado como agente conversacional. Se concluye que KG-RAG Dinámico amplía eficazmente el paradigma RAG y es aplicable a sistemas que requieren memoria estructurada, persistente y evolutiva.

title: Explainable Multimodal Artificial Intelligence for Precision Laboratory Diagnosis: Integrating Biomarkers, Molecular Profiles, Immunological Signatures, and Clinical Data
abstract: Background: Precision laboratory diagnosis increasingly relies on the interpretation of heterogeneous biological and clinical information. Conventional workflows tend to examine biomarkers, molecular measurements, immunological findings, and clinical characteristics along partly separate analytical pathways. Artificial intelligence (AI) can uncover complex relationships in high-dimensional biomedical data, yet many such systems remain hard to interpret at the point of clinical use. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) renders algorithmic outputs more transparent by identifying the features, modalities, and interactions that shape a prediction. Objective: This manuscript proposes an explainable multimodal AI framework for precision laboratory diagnosis, termed XMAI-PLD, which unites conventional laboratory biomarkers, molecular profiles, immunological signatures, and clinical data within a single analytical architecture. The framework is designed to support, rather than supplant, laboratory expertise and clinical judgement. Framework: The architecture comprises seven interconnected layers: data acquisition; quality control and harmonisation; modality-specific representation; multimodal fusion; diagnostic inference; explainability and uncertainty assessment; and laboratory–clinical decision support. Biomarker measurements contribute quantitative biochemical information, molecular profiles characterise genomic or molecular alterations, immunological signatures capture host-response patterns, and clinical variables supply patient-level context. Each stream is processed separately before being integrated through multimodal learning, and explanations are generated at the modality and feature levels to reveal the principal drivers of each output. Clinical and Laboratory Relevance: The framework addresses the shortcomings of isolated single-modality models, namely incomplete biological representation, heterogeneous data structures, missing information, analytical variability, and limited interpretability. Its proposed outputs comprise diagnostic probabilities, contributing features, modality-level evidence, uncertainty estimates, and cases flagged for human review. Particular emphasis falls on analytical validity, calibration, external validation, data provenance, subgroup assessment, cybersecurity, privacy, and human oversight. Conclusion: Explainable multimodal AI offers a promising route towards a more integrated diagnostic representation of laboratory and clinical evidence. Its worth will hinge not only on predictive performance but also on analytical robustness, reproducibility, interpretability, calibration, clinical usefulness, and sustained human oversight. Prospective, multicentre evaluation is required before such systems enter routine diagnostic practice.

title: Student Psychology-Based Optimization Algorithm Enhanced by Teaching–Learning Mechanism for Global Optimization and Real-World Issues
abstract: Student Psychology-Based Optimization (SPBO) provides a simple human-inspired search framework, but its dependence on random subject-wise learning behaviors, limited peer interaction, and insufficient utilization of historical information may restrict its performance on complex multimodal optimization problems. To address these limitations, this study proposes a Multi-Strategy Improved Student Psychology-Based Optimization algorithm, termed MLSPBO. Three complementary learning mechanisms are incorporated into the original framework. First, a multi-teacher hierarchical guidance strategy constructs a rank-weighted collective teaching reference to reduce excessive dependence on a single elite individual and provide diversified search directions. Second, a rank-adaptive peer mutual-learning strategy enables individuals with different performance levels to adopt differentiated learning behaviors, thereby enhancing information exchange and population diversity. Third, a self-reflection and remedial learning strategy exploits historical best information and search stagnation to strengthen local refinement and escape from unfavorable regions. The performance of MLSPBO is evaluated on the CEC2020 and CEC2022 benchmark suites under 10- and 20-dimensional settings and compared with nine representative metaheuristic algorithms. MLSPBO obtains the best or tied-best mean results on 7/10 and 9/10 CEC2020 functions and on 11/12 functions under both CEC2022 settings. Its Friedman mean ranks are 1.30, 1.10, 1.33, and 1.17, respectively, consistently ranking first among all compared methods. In addition, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test yields an aggregated 39 wins, 3 ties, and 2 losses against the original SPBO. The practical performance of MLSPBO was further evaluated using a three-dimensional robotic arm path planning problem. Its mean cost was 291.34, approximately 5.44% lower than that obtained by NDO and 6.10% lower than that of the original SPBO. The results suggest that the proposed method is not limited to numerical benchmark optimization and can also provide reliable solutions for constrained robotic path-planning tasks.

title: Understanding preferences for explainable AI: A study on LIME variations
abstract: The current research aims to empirically examine user preferences of four variations of visual explanations from an image classification model. Participants (N = 23) were recruited from a Midwestern university. The study was a within-subjects design in which participants were asked to rate four local interpretable model-agnostic explanation (LIME) variations from best to worst in an image classification task across 10 trials. A Friedman's test and a Plackett-Luce analysis were conducted to examine participants' rank-order preferences for the variations, and a linear mixed-effects model on eye-tracking data was used to examine on which variations participants expended the most visual effort. Results reveal that, overall, participants preferred images that were non-obfuscated and spent more time fixating on images that highlighted both positive and negative features compared to positive only features. The findings have implications for interface design, particularly for designers aiming to prioritize human-centered preferences.
